Every member agrees it with the rest of the record. It closes this unit's section of your Capstone S2R Blueprint and guides the assessors through your work."

slides.title: Step 1 · The 3S Check
slides.notes:
SECTION 5 · STEP 1 — THE 3S CHECK (CAPSTONE WORK)

HOW TO TEACH IT:
1. Brief the step.
Say: "Your page shows the Start and Stop lists your group confirmed in Unit 3.
These are the changes your strategy asks of people.
Your group states one Shift, one Stake and one Step for the strategy."

2. Teach each of the three with its guide.
The guide beside each box is the lesson of 1.3.1.
Shift · “What is changing?”
What it is: The Shift names the practice that ends and the practice that begins, for a named group, from a named date. 
It is concrete enough to be observed: someone watching the work could tell whether it is happening. 
A direction such as “more customer-focused” leaves every person to decide what it means, and each will decide differently.
Weak: “We are becoming more customer-focused.”
Clear: “From March, agents resolve complaints on the first call.”
Leader’s move: State the Shift as from and to: what stops, what starts, for whom, from when.
The group answers: What is changing?

Stake · “What do we gain if we change, and what do we lose if we stay as we are?”
What it is: The Stake is why the change matters, and it has two sides. The gain says what the change is for. The loss says what standing still will cost. Both are needed, because people weigh a loss more heavily than an equal gain. A change described only by its benefits leaves the people affected holding the one visible loss: the practice they are asked to give up. Naming what is lost by staying put places a second loss on the scales. The Stake is stated in terms the affected group cares about. An enterprise benefit that never reaches their work reads as someone else’s reason.
Weak: “It supports our strategy.”
Clear: “We keep the customers who now leave after a two-day wait. If we stay as we are, we keep losing them.”
Leader’s move: State the gain and the loss together, in the group’s own terms.
The group answers: What will the organisation gain if it changes, and what will it lose if it stays as it is?

Step · “What do I do differently?”
What it is: The Step is the person’s own part. It is said in the first person and is small enough to do next week. The Shift belongs to the organisation and the Step belongs to the person, so each role affected needs its own. A change with a clear Shift and no Step is understood as something that will happen to other people.
Weak: “Embrace the new process.”
Clear: “I decide on the call, within my limit.”
Leader’s move: Give each affected role its own Step, and ask people to say it back.
The group answers: What must be done differently?

3. Bridge to Step 2.
Say: "With the change stated, Step 2 names the leadership behaviours that will hold it in place."


ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants work as a group in Step 1 of Section 5 of the participant file. This is Capstone work.
1. The group reads the practices the strategy starts and stops. Each page shows the Start and Stop lists the group confirmed in Unit 3.
2. The group reads the guide in each card. It is the lesson from part 1.3.1.
3. The group agrees its Shift, Stake and Step for the strategy, and each participant writes them in the three boxes.

LATER, WHEN THE GROUPS DO THE WORK ON THE PORTAL:
The group chooses its scribe for this work. The scribe types what the group agrees, and the entries appear on every member’s page.
Guide each group to test each statement against its guide. A statement that could be said of any organisation has not yet been written for this strategy.
The Shift: the group states what stops, what starts, for whom and from when. The Stake: the group states the gain and what the organisation loses if it stays as it is. The Step: each member states their own part in the first person.

slides.title: Step 2 · ACE-IT
slides.notes:
SECTION 5 · STEP 2 — ACE-IT (CAPSTONE WORK)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Open with the team’s OCEAVL profile.
Say: "Your page shows your team’s OCEAVL profile: the team’s level on each dimension, with its risk and its response.
It appears once every member of your team has submitted their scores in part 3.1."
Where a member has not yet submitted, the profile shows how many have. The group completes 3.1 first.

Deepen, say: "The same input lands differently depending on the ground it falls on.
When a change initiative fails to take, the reflex is to blame the message.
First diagnose the conditions stopping good input from rooting."
(Insight: Diagnose the soil. Source: Journal, 21 May 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

2. Name the two highest-risk dimensions.
Say: "From your team’s profile, your group names the two dimensions on which your executive team carries the highest risk for the strategy, and the response your team adopts for each.
The profile gives the risk and the response at your team’s level."
Ask: "Which level in your team’s profile carries the highest risk for this change? Which ACE-IT behaviour answers it?"

3. Teach each of the five behaviours with its guide.
The guide beside each box is the lesson of 1.3.4.
Accountability
Definition: Taking full ownership for results. Acknowledging missteps and driving corrective action.
What it does for a new practice: One named person owns the practice and its result.
Observable: Commitments tracked • Reviews end with named owners • “We missed it, here’s the fix” language common

Commitment
Definition: Staying anchored to agreed strategic intent even when pressure rises. Following through despite discomfort.
What it does for a new practice: The practice is kept when pressure rises and the old way is quicker.
Observable: Strategic priorities stay consistent • Leaders decline non-strategic work • Promises kept visibly

Engagement
Definition: Actively involving self and others in sense-making, dialogue, and execution. Listening to understand.
What it does for a new practice: People talk about how it is going and improve it together.
Observable: Team meetings are two-way • Feedback loops visible • People quote the shared “why”

Integrity
Definition: Acting consistently with values, facts, and truth — even when inconvenient. Declaring conflicts of interest early.
What it does for a new practice: Slips are reported as they are, and early.
Observable: Evidence cited before decisions • Values referenced in hard choices • Teams trust word matches deed

Transparency
Definition: Making reasoning, progress, and constraints visible to all stakeholders. Sharing challenges openly.
What it does for a new practice: Its results are visible to everyone the change affects.
Observable: Dashboards updated regularly • Decisions logged and accessible • “No surprises” culture evident

For each behaviour the group writes: the behaviour we expect from our leadership team.

4. Give the example.

EXAMPLE
The team’s level on Agreeableness is High.
Risk: Agreement given without genuine commitment; team over-commits; resentment builds beneath surface harmony.
Expected behaviour under Commitment: “Each of us states our capacity before we accept new work for this change.”

5. Bridge to the Unit Summary.
Say: "With the change and the behaviours stated, we close the unit."

LATER, WHEN THE GROUPS DO THE WORK ON THE PORTAL:
The group opens with its team OCEAVL profile. Where a member has not yet submitted, the profile shows how many have; that member completes 3.1 first.
Each behaviour: the group writes what a colleague would see the leadership team do. A value such as “we will be accountable” becomes a behaviour once it is stated that way.
Whose behaviour: the five boxes hold the leadership team’s own behaviour.

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants work as a group in Step 2 of Section 5 of the participant file. This is Capstone work.
1. The group reads its team OCEAVL profile, shown on each page once every member of the team has submitted their scores in part 3.1.
2. The group names the two dimensions on which its executive team carries the highest risk for the strategy, and the response it adopts for each.
3. The group reads the guide in each card. It is the lesson from part 1.3.4.
4. For each behaviour, the group agrees what it expects to see the leadership team do so that the change in Step 1 holds. Where the team’s level carries a risk for this change, the group states the behaviour that answers it.
5. Each participant reads the record and selects Agree. Print gives a copy of the record.

WHERE THE RECORD GOES:
The agreed record feeds boxes 5A to 5C of the team’s Capstone S2R® Blueprint: the two highest-risk dimensions in 5A, the Shift, Stake and Step in 5B, the expected leadership behaviours in 5C.

UNIT SUMMARY (UNIT 5 SYNTHESIS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Recap the unit, section by section.
Say: "This session was about the human conditions that decide whether a strategy ever moves.
Aligning Heart & Mind treated execution as first a human problem: strategy moves through people before it moves through systems."
- 1 · Awareness: strategy enters through Cognition (Mind) and Emotion (Heart). Five principles describe how alignment is created and sustained.
- 2 · Intelligence: Heart & Mind alignment is the ignition point that converts strategic potential energy into kinetic energy. Compliance yields short-term output. Commitment sustains execution when leaders are not present.
- 3 · Extrapolating: each participant completes the OCEAVL Assessment across seven dimensions. The level held by most members is the team’s level, and every level carries a risk, a response and three routines.
- 4 · Integration: the leadership team leads change with one voice through four commitments. Each CXO role brings a Converging Zone Contribution and carries an Alignment Hot Zone.
- 5 · Application: each group states its Shift, Stake and Step for the strategy, reads its team OCEAVL profile, names its two highest-risk dimensions with the response to each, and states the ACE-IT behaviours it expects from the leadership team.
- Across the unit: a change is adopted when it passes the 4 Checks of Mind, Heart, Hands and Habit. The leader’s job is to explain, involve, equip and reinforce until it passes all four.

2. Ask the closing question on the slide.
Ask: "Which ACE-IT behaviour in your record will be hardest for this leadership team to show, and what in the team’s OCEAVL profile makes it so?"
Take an answer from each group.

3. Close the unit.
Say: "Aligned hearts and minds turn a strategy from a document the organisation has read into a direction the organisation is willing to move on."
Say: "Each group has stated the change and the leadership behaviours that will hold it in place."

4. Bridge to Unit 6.
Say: "Unit 6 builds the system that connects enterprise results to the contributions of people and the conditions the organisation provides."


ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants complete every part of the participant file: the thirteen reflections, the OCEAVL Assessment and the group’s record in Section 5. When the page is complete, each participant submits the unit to the facilitator from the end of Section 5.
